newsitem.title: UK: Dollar ends European session just below 1.69 marks.
newsitem.headline: Dollar ends European session just below 1.69 marks.

text.p: The dollar soared in late Europe, less than two hours after plummeting on data showing a ballooning U.S. trade gap, as comments by Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan fuelled rate hike expectations.
"Greenspan is still holding out the idea of a pre-emptive move," said Tony Norfield, treasury economist at ABN AMRO.
"It is clear the economy is growing strongly and that is the environment in which you would expect a pre-emptive rate hike," said Norfield.
At 1550 GMT the dollar was trading at 1.6846/51 marks against 1.6816/10 in late Europe on Wednesday and well above lows of 1.6708.
Against the yen, the dollar stood at 123.55/3.61 yen at 1604 GMT against 122.69 yen in late Europe on Wednesday and well off session lows at 122.19 yen.

In the U.S. Wall Street shares and bonds fell after a raft of comments on the state of the economy and inflation, delivered in prepared testimony by Greenspan to Congress's Joint Economic Committee, spooked those markets in anticipation of higher U.S. rates.
"It looks like he is preparing the ground for some pre-emptive action," said Jeremy Stretch, currency strategist at NatWest Markets.

The central bank's policy-making Federal Open Market Committee meets on Tuesday to consider raising short-term rates. "Should we choose to alter monetary policy, we know from past experience that, although the financial markets may respond immediately, the main effects on inflationary pressures may not be felt until late this year and in 1998," Greenspan said on Thursday. And, as he has done before, he stressed the importance of the Fed acting promptly to keep inflation low. "While inflation may not be a problem at the moment, tightness in labour markets, wages does suggest that a pre-emptive strike is probable," said Stretch. A stronger-than-forecast 17.4 reading in the February Philly Fed index against January's 11.3 added fresh fuel to the belief the Fed will raise rates, said analysts.

Earlier, however, the dollar was slapped to lows of 1.6708 marks and 122.19 yen after U.S. data showed the trade gap soared for a second consecutive month in January to hit its highest level in nearly 10 years.

"I think it's clearly a surprising figure," said Adam Chester, international analyst at Yamaichi International, after data showed the gap swelling 21.1 percent to $12.7 bln in January and much higher than forecasts for a gap of $10.7 bln.
In other currencies, the mark ended the session a touch softer on its European crosses, aided by dollar/mark's rally, while mark/lira dipped below 1001 lire after the release of March inflation data.
Earlier the Geman unit sank to 1997 lows against the Swiss franc. The mark dipped to as low as 85.43 centimes, its lowest level since 85.42 on December 18.
